name: Amira Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm usually on the 7:40 bus to the hospital campus for lectures in anatomy and nursing practice. Afternoons are skills lab, where we practise things like taking blood pressure on each other. I share a flat with three people near the ring road, and on Saturdays and Sundays I work the counter at a pharmacy. I love the lab days. The reading wears me out, because I do everything on paper and the folders are piling up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can see what the degree is for. My mum (a care assistant) has done night shifts for twenty years, and I want to be the one who has a say on the ward. What wears me out is money maths on Sunday nights. Fees are covered by my loan, but rent and the uniform and the placement travel are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say I told you so. Everyone shouted about robots and chatbots for years, and then it turns out to be a slightly better spell checker. I'd say it at the pharmacy too, where the new stock-ordering screen has already made one more job for us, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm relieved but not relaxed. Nursing will still need people at the bedside. What I really think is that my worries are the old ones: my share of the rent, my loan, and whether I'll get a placement near home so I don't pay for two trains a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Keep my Saturday and Sunday shifts, keep writing notes by hand, and put about forty pounds a month into the savings account my dad opened for me. I'd also join the student nursing society, because they have a hardship fund for placement travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, like a normal bad-weather week. Not scary, just tiring. I'd still be counting money, and I don't think a world where nothing changes fixes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use these tools. Does that cost you anything in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you never use these tools. Does that cost you anything in this picture?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the pharmacy cuts shifts anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, because in this picture nobody needs them. My flatmate Priya uses a chatbot to summarise articles and she says it saves her an hour. I'd rather read the article myself, because I remember it better. If it turns out I'm slower, then I'm slower. I can live with that for a few years.

say: I'd say **told you so**: all that hype and we got a slightly better spell checker.
I'd tell friends my **real worries** are rent and placement travel, not robots.
think: I'm relieved, but my **loan and rent** keep me up more than AI ever did.
Nursing stays a **people job**, so I feel fairly safe about the degree.
do: **Keep** both weekend pharmacy shifts and my hand-written study routine.
**Save** forty pounds a month into the account my dad opened.
**Join** the nursing society to use its placement hardship fund.
feel: Steady and tired, like a **normal** bad-weather week, still counting money.
S0.quote: Everyone shouted about robots and chatbots for years, and then it turns out to be a slightly better spell checker.
fieldNote: Amira's **money worries** are ordinary and already present; AI barely registers.
She is relieved, not carefree: the loan and placement costs keep her **uneasy**.
Her refusal to use AI tools is a **principle**, not fear; she says she remembers paper better.

steps.text: Keep both weekend pharmacy counter shifts
Pay forty pounds a month into the savings account
Apply to the nursing society's placement travel hardship fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time somebody asked who this is good for. If software is going to take the paperwork off nurses, great, but the hospital should use the time to hire more people on wards, not cut. At the pharmacy I already see the screen doing the checking that used to be a person's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think nursing is safe for me but not comfortable. The thinking jobs go first, so my dad's depot office and the clerks at the hospital might lose theirs. My mum is hands-on so she'd be fine for longer. Mostly I'd worry that I graduate into a ward that uses the new tools to run with fewer staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the one thing I've been avoiding, which is to learn what these systems do on a ward, because I'd rather be able to argue about them. I'd ask my tutor for a module on health tech, and I'd join the union branch for student nurses. I'd keep my weekend shifts, though I'd watch whether the pharmacy still wants two people at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing in a river that's rising slowly. I'm not drowning, but I can't pretend the water isn't coming up. It makes me a bit angry at the companies that rush this out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union branch actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the union branch actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if wards end up with fewer staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it gives a bunch of us a louder voice before the hospital decides things. Last term the branch got placement travel refunded within a month, which an individual student would never manage. If staffing rules get written around these tools, I want a student nurse in the room. It's slow, boring work, and I'm more likely to turn up than most.

say: I'd say **who benefits**: use saved time to hire ward staff, not cut them.
I'd tell friends the pharmacy screen already does **checking** a person used to do.
think: Nursing is **safe but not comfortable**; I fear I graduate into a ward with fewer staff.
My dad's depot office and **hospital clerks** may go first, before my mum's hands-on care work.
do: **Ask** my tutor about a health-technology module this year.
**Join** the student nurses' union branch within the first term.
**Watch** whether the pharmacy still staffs two people on weekends.
feel: Like a **slowly rising** river: not drowning yet, and a bit angry at firms rushing it.
S1.quote: If staffing rules get written around these tools, I want a student nurse in the room.
fieldNote: She turns worry into **collective action** quickly; the union is her instinct, not a last resort.
Her anger points at **companies and employers**, not at the technology.
She still avoids the tools herself but now wants to **understand** them well enough to argue.

steps.text: Ask the tutor for a health technology module
Join the student nurses' union branch
Keep the weekend pharmacy shifts for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules before it arrives, not after. Two years is nothing. Governments have a track record of arriving late, and I'd say that loudly, probably at the next union meeting and in the group chat with my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly this one scares me, not for my own nursing but for my dad. My dad is a delivery driver, and if robots do hands-on work from 2031, his job is next. I'd graduate in 2029, and my first two years on the ward could be the ones where he's out of work and I'm the earner with a student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by sitting down with my parents and writing down what we owe and what we'd do if Dad's route disappeared. I'd take extra pharmacy shifts now, maybe three days a week instead of two, and push my savings up. I'd also ask the university what support exists, and I'd write to my local councillor about retraining money for drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels tight in my chest. I keep thinking about my dad at the kitchen table with his van keys. I'd try to be the calm one at home, but I wouldn't feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you actually bring this up with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you actually bring this up with your dad?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if your studies and the family budget collide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until Sunday lunch, when he's relaxed, and I'd say it plainly: I'm not saying it will happen, but I'd like us to have a plan. He'll joke and wave it away, and my mum will go quiet. Then she'll bring it up again later, because she always does. I'd offer to cover some of my own costs so he doesn't have to worry about me.

say: I'd say we need **rules before it arrives**, because two years is nothing.
I'd say governments **arrive late**, loudly, at the union meeting and in the family group chat.
think: My real fear is my dad: a delivery driver whose job could go around **2031**.
I might graduate in 2029 as the **main earner** with a student loan.
do: **Sit down** with my parents to list debts and a plan if Dad's route goes.
**Work** three pharmacy days a week instead of two, to build savings.
**Write** to my local councillor about retraining money for drivers.
feel: A **tight chest**, picturing Dad at the kitchen table with his van keys.
S2.quote: My dad is a delivery driver, and if robots do hands-on work from 2031, his job is next.
fieldNote: Her fear is **for her father**, not herself; household income is what moves her to anxious.
She plans to be the **calm one** at home while feeling the opposite.
She jumps to **politics and family planning**, not to AI tools.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and list what we owe
Work three pharmacy days a week to build savings
Write to my local councillor about retraining money for drivers
Ask the university what hardship support exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible and short enough that nobody's allowed to dither. I'd say it to my union branch: we need guaranteed retraining for people whose jobs go, paid for by the firms that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calmer than in the two-year picture but still on edge. I'd have qualified by 2029, and then I'd have two years as a nurse before robots reach hands-on work at all. Nursing is about touch and judgment, so I'd probably be okay. Dad is the worry again, and he'd have time to change if he starts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and I'd try to pick a first job in a big hospital with a union, not a small private home. I'd ask Dad to look at the training courses for warehouse supervisors or van maintenance, and I'd help him fill in the forms. I'd keep saving about sixty pounds a month, so I'd have six weeks of rent by the time I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long grey winter, but one with an end. I can plan inside it, which makes it much easier than the two-year picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those five years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training that's paid for, not just a leaflet. I'd want a guaranteed place on a course for any worker who's lost a job, with enough money to cover the rent while they do it. My mum would also say care workers should be paid properly, because everyone will need care when thinking jobs vanish. I'd vote for whoever promises it and means it.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough to act**: guaranteed retraining, paid for by firms that profit.
I'd tell my union branch nobody is allowed to **dither** now.
think: I'd qualify by 2029 and nurse for **two years** before robots reach hands-on work.
Dad is the worry again, but he'd have **time** to change if he starts early.
do: **Aim** for a first job at a big unionised hospital, not a small private home.
**Help** Dad apply for supervisor or van-maintenance training courses.
**Save** about sixty pounds a month, to have six weeks of rent by graduation.
feel: A **long grey winter** with an end, which I can plan inside.
S3.quote: I'd want a guaranteed place on a course for any worker who's lost a job, with enough money to cover the rent while they do it.
fieldNote: Time lowers her fear but she stays **anxious** because her father's job is still the weak point.
Policy answers are **concrete**: paid courses, rent cover, proper care pay.
She links her own career **choices** (large unionised hospital) to AI risk.

steps.text: Aim for a first nursing job in a large unionised hospital
Help Dad fill in forms for van maintenance training
Save sixty pounds a month before graduation
Vote for parties that promise paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we just keep arguing. I'd say it in the student union and online, because it's the only picture where regulation, training and union deals can all happen before the big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel lighter. By 2036 I'd be about thirty, with a few years on the ward behind me. Mum would be near retirement and Dad close to it too, so their jobs would matter less. My own worry would be whether care jobs get squeezed by budgets even if robots don't take them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study as planned and do the extras that make me hard to replace, like a diploma in a specialism such as palliative care. I'd start paying into a pension at my first job, even a little. I'd join a campaign for safe staffing levels in my first year as a nurse. And I might finally try one of the AI tools, just to know what I'm arguing against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels almost calm, though I don't trust that calm. A decade is a long time, and I'm young enough to believe I'll cope with most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why might you finally try one of the tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why might you finally try one of the tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family's situation look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have the time and no excuse. If I'm going to lobby about staffing rules, I should know what the software does for real, not just what the news says. I'd try it on something harmless, like planning my study timetable. I won't love it, but being able to say I've used it makes my argument stronger.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if we use it for training and regulation.
I'd say it in the student union: arguing is a **waste** of the time we have.
think: By 2036 I'd be about thirty with a few years on the ward, and my parents **near retirement**.
My worry is **budgets** squeezing care jobs even if robots never take them.
do: **Study** a specialism such as palliative care to make myself hard to replace.
**Start** paying into a pension at my first job, even a small amount.
**Try** an AI tool once, on something harmless like my timetable.
feel: Almost **calm**, though I don't fully trust that calm.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we just keep arguing.
fieldNote: The long runway **softens** her mood; her parents' retirement ages remove the household earner worry.
Her **first willingness** to try an AI tool appears here, framed as better argument.
She trusts **institutions** only if pushed by unions and campaigns.

steps.text: Take a palliative care diploma after qualifying
Start paying into a pension at my first job
Join a safe staffing campaign in my first year on the ward
Try one AI tool on my study timetable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it lands on my dad and on my first years as a nurse at the same time. What would help is a guaranteed paid retraining place for anyone who loses work, and a rule that hospitals can't use new software to cut ward staff. Also proper pay for care workers, because we'll all need them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume nursing students are naive. We aren't. We see how thin the staffing already is, and that's why I'm cautious about anyone promising that technology will fix it.

headlineQuote: We see how thin the staffing already is, and that's why I'm cautious about anyone promising that technology will fix it.
portrait: Amira is **nineteen**, a first-year nursing student who shares a flat and works weekends at a pharmacy counter.
She is **progressive** and union-minded, with a mum in care work and a dad who drives a delivery van.
She avoids AI tools on principle and writes notes by hand, so her answer is **organise and regulate**.
She stays uneasy when little changes and becomes **anxious** in the fast scenarios because of her dad's job.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most, landing on her dad's job and her first years as a nurse.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **paid retraining** place for anyone who loses work, plus rules stopping hospitals cutting ward staff.
